\begin{center}
{\Large MATH 147 --- Proof Practice}\\[2pt]
Lectures 7--12 \quad Fall 2026
\end{center}

\noindent Attempt each problem before looking at the hints in lecture. Write complete proofs.

\section*{Lecture 7 --- Convergence and Boundedness}

\noindent\textbf{Problem 1.} Prove directly from the definition that
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{3n+1}{n+2} = 3.
\]

\noindent\textbf{Problem 2.} Let $(x_n)$ be a convergent sequence. Prove that $(x_n)$ is bounded, that is, there exists $M > 0$ with $|x_n| \le M$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

\section*{Lecture 8 --- Algebra of Limits}

\noindent\textbf{Problem 3.} Suppose $x_n \to x$ and $y_n \to y$. Prove that $x_n y_n \to xy$ using the triangle inequality.

\noindent\textbf{Problem 4.} Let $x_n \to L$ with $L > 0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
  \item Show that there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n > L/2$ for all $n \ge N$.
  \item Deduce that $\sqrt{x_n} \to \sqrt{L}$.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lecture 9 --- Monotone Sequences}

\noindent\textbf{Problem 5.} Define $x_1 = 1$ and $x_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + x_n}$ for $n \ge 1$. Prove that the recursive sequence $(x_n)$ is increasing and bounded, and find its limit.

\noindent\textbf{Problem 6.} Let $a_n = \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n$. Show that $(a_n)$ is increasing and bounded above by $3$, and conclude that it converges.

\section*{Lecture 10 --- Subsequences}

\noindent\textbf{Problem 7.} Prove that if every subsequence of $(x_n)$ has a further subsequence converging to $L$, then $x_n \to L$.

\section*{Lecture 11 --- Bolzano--Weierstrass}

\noindent\textbf{Problem 8.} Use the Bolzano--Weierstrass theorem to show that every bounded sequence $(x_n)$ has a convergent subsequence whose limit lies in the interval $[\inf_n x_n, \sup_n x_n]$.

\section*{Lecture 12 --- Cauchy Sequences}

\noindent\textbf{Problem 9.} Suppose $|x_{n+1} - x_n| \le 2^{-n}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence.

\noindent\textbf{Problem 10.} For bounded sequences $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$, prove that
\[
  \limsup_{n\to\infty} (x_n + y_n) \le \limsup_{n\to\infty} x_n + \limsup_{n\to\infty} y_n.
\]
